extracted.intended_audience: British legislators and the politically engaged public (late-18th-century readers and policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: A political-philosophical critique of a proposed constitution (the French scheme) that articulates standards and failings for legislative, executive, judicial, and military institutions. Emphasises institutional design principles such as checks and balances, judicial independence, executive dignity, and military discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate / advisory council
rubrics_metrics.description: “They have forgot to constitute a _senate_, or something of that nature and character.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A middle body (senate/council) is essential in a republic: something foreign states may connect with, something the people may look up to, that gives bias, steadiness, and preserves consistency in the proceedings of state. Its absence is a sovereign incapacity in framers of a constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive must have deliberative discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed executive is “a machine, without any sort of deliberative discretion in any one act of his function.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An executive reduced to a mere channel or notary cannot direct measures effectively; the office of execution is an office of exertion and requires genuine discretion to perform duties faithfully and usefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive dignity, authority, and rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: “It ought to be environed with dignity, authority, and consideration, and it ought to lead to glory.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure zealous service the executive must have means to reward (honor, offices, pensions, land) and be a fountain of honor; lacking these, servants of the executive act from fear alone, undermining loyal and effective administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive role in justice (fountain of justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The king of France is not the fountain of justice. The judges... are of his nomination. He... is not even the public prosecutor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depriving the executive of ordinary judicial prerogatives (origination of process, suspension, mitigation, pardon) renders the office degrading and ineffective; some judicial and clemency functions are tied to the dignity and authority of the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive prerogative over peace and war (foreign policy powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The framers might have left to the king “the right of peace and war.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although hazardous, vesting the executive with the prerogative of peace and war can prevent foreign potentates from personally intriguing with legislators and helps centralise conduct of foreign affairs; such powers should be balanced with auxiliary trusts and correctives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent judiciary / permanent tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: The old parliaments “possessed one fundamental excellence: they were independent... They held for life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent, independent tribunals supply certainty and stability to the laws, protect private property, act as a corrective to sudden democratic decrees, and preserve the memory and consistency of the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence from legislative instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are to be “sworn to obey all the rules, orders, and instructions which from time to time they are to receive from the National Assembly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binding judges to obey ad hoc legislative instructions leaves no ground of law to the subject, permits the governing power to change rules mid-cause, and makes judges dangerous instruments of faction; judges must not be subordinated to legislative fiat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve remonstrance/registration powers
rubrics_metrics.description: It would have been prudent “to preserve their ancient power of registering, and of remonstrating... as they did upon those which passed in the time of the monarchy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration and remonstrance powers enable a tribunal to square occasional decrees to general jurisprudence and control the excesses of a democracy; removing these powers reduces checks on legislative acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid elective, temporary, local judges
rubrics_metrics.description: “Elective, temporary, local judges, such as you have contrived, exercising their dependent functions in a narrow society, must be the worst of all tribunals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary/local elective judges are prone to faction, partiality toward neighbors, suspicion from ballots, and inability to protect strangers, minorities, or the rich; judicial selection should favour permanence and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative bodies must be subject to law
rubrics_metrics.description: “The administrative bodies are carefully exempted from the jurisdiction of these new tribunals... Those who execute public pecuniary trusts ought of all men to be the most strictly held to their duty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative/administrative-corporate officers should not be placed above the law; they must be coercible and accountable via tribunals so that public trusts are enforceable and constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid parallel real and fictitious establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: You have settled “two establishments of government,—one real, one fictitious: both maintained at a vast expense; but the fictitious at, I think, the greatest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not maintain pageants or ceremonial institutions without real authority; align form with function, create instruments useful to ends, and avoid exorbitant expense for mere show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative limits, fundamental laws, and rules of proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Assembly is “a body in its constitution with every possible power and no possible external control... without fundamental laws, without established maxims, without respected rules of proceeding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sovereign legislature must be constrained by fundamental laws, established maxims and procedural rules to avoid arbitrary, inconsistent, and ever-changing governance; separation and limits are essential to stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military as instrument under civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: “The nature of things requires that the army should never act but as an instrument. The moment that... it shall act according to its own resolutions, _the government... will immediately degenerate into a military democracy_.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The army must remain disciplined and subordinate to civil command; chiefs must retain authority, soldiers must not form independent committees, and insubordination (murders of commanders, removal of colors, etc.) must be suppressed to prevent military rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers must have real power, discretion, and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers “are to execute, without power; they are to be responsible, without discretion; they are to deliberate, without choice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility alone deters crime but does not motivate zeal or wise administration; ministers require discretion, means, and incentives to perform duties effectively rather than merely being blameable scapegoats.

rubrics_metrics.name: High state judicature must be independent and not partisan
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed “grand state judicature... subservient to their inquisition, _the Committee of Research_, will extinguish the last sparks of liberty... They must not evoke from or send to it the causes relative to their own members, at their pleasure. They must also remove the seat of that tribunal out of the republic of Paris.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A supreme court for state offences must not be under the control of the governing assembly or its investigative committee, must not try the assembly’s own members at its whim, and should be located and constituted to avoid local partisan domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of law: avoid ruling by occasional decrees (psephismata)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vice of ancient democracies was “that they ruled, as you do, by occasional decrees, _psephismata_. This practice soon broke in upon the tenor and consistency of the laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should aim for continuity, coherence and general jurisprudence rather than frequent ad hoc decrees; short laws that leave excessive discretion to judges are also problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect judges' safety and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges “sit under a guard to save their own lives... when they acquit, we know they have seen the persons whom they discharge, with perfect impunity to the actors, hanged at the door of their court.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges must be free from fear of violent retaliation; the judicial office must be protected so that acquittals and judgments are respected, and judges do not feel compelled to condemn at peril of their lives.
